title: Northrop books sixth Falcon 9 for Cygnus as Antares 330 waits - NASASpaceFlight.com
html:
Northrop Grumman has contracted a sixth Falcon 9 launch for its Cygnus resupply spacecraft, extending its reliance on SpaceX while its own Antares 330 remains unavailable.

The update came during a pre-launch media teleconference on Monday ahead of the NG-25 mission scheduled to launch Nov. 29 from Cape Canaveral.

Dave Schiller, vice president of civil space and sciences at Northrop Grumman, confirmed the additional Falcon 9 slot.

“We do have one additional Falcon 9 on the manifest for Cygnus,” he said.

Ahead of this week's NG-25 mission, we've got some news on Cygnus.

After five missions on Falcon 9, @NorthropGrumman announces they have added a sixth to the manifest. This means its own Antares 330 is not yet ready.

While there weren't any updates of substance on Antares, Dave… pic.twitter.com/eyCndQmnmE

— Ryan Caton (@dpoddolphinpro) November 23, 2026

NG-25 is the fifth Cygnus to fly on Falcon 9 since the retirement of the Antares 230+, following NG-20, NG-21, NG-23 and NG-24. The new contract adds a sixth Falcon 9 flight after those, a clear sign that Antares 330 will not be ready for the near-term manifest.

Antares 330 timeline unclear

Schiller described progress on the new vehicle in general terms.

“We are making meaningful progress in the development of A330 as we call it, but as with any complex launch vehicle program, schedules can evolve as development and testing continue. We will share any additional details about availability as they become available.”

No further information was provided on hardware status, engine testing, or a first flight target.

Antares 330 render by NSF’s Mack Crawford

Schiller added that Northrop continues to work with NASA and other providers to avoid any gaps in Cygnus flights.

“As we look further out into the flight plan, we always work dynamically with NASA and others to identify launch vehicle opportunities as we assess the readiness of the launch vehicle market,” he said.

“So we continually plan forward, and we do not anticipate a gap in any of the launch provider launch manifests for Cygnus.”

No update on NG-22

NSF’s Ryan Caton asked about NG-22, the Cygnus that never made it to the launch pad.

In March 2025, Northrop informed NASA that the shipping container carrying NG-22’s Pressurized Cargo Module (PCM) was damaged while being shipped to the launch site.

A shipping container with the next Cygnus Pressurized Cargo Module inside has been damaged.

NASA Statement:

"NASA’s International Space Station Program and Northrop Grumman are assessing potential mission impacts to the company’s next commercial resupply flight currently…

— NSF – NASASpaceflight.com (@NASASpaceflight) March 5, 2025

Thales Alenia Space built the PCM in Turin, Italy, and shipped it to the United States for integration with the Cygnus service module.

Later that month, NASA confirmed that inspections had found damage to the cargo module itself. The June 2025 mission was called off, and NG-23 moved up to become Northrop’s next flight to the station.

NASA said at the time that it would continue working with Northrop to assess whether the module could safely fly on a future mission.

At the NG-23 pre-launch media teleconference on Sept. 12, 2025, Ryan Tintner, Vice President of Civil Space Systems at Northrop Grumman, said: “We’re still working through that, but NG-22 will fly.

“NG-22 mission will be manifested, and we’re working with NASA to determine, as we complete the path forward there, exactly what the timing will be.”

NG-25 Cygnus leaving Turin – Credit: Thales Alenia Space

More than a year later, Schiller had little new to share.

“No, not a lot more information. We do plan to fly NG-22, and it will be rescheduled once the repairs are made to the pressurized cargo module. But we don’t have any other updates at this time.”

That leaves NG-22 as an open item in Northrop’s Cygnus sequence, with no target date for its return to the manifest.

NG-25 proceeds on Falcon 9

NG-25 will launch on Falcon 9 from Space Launch Complex 40 (SLC-40).

The Cygnus XL spacecraft, named the S.S. James “Jim” A. Lovell, is carrying approximately 11,000 pounds of cargo, science experiments, and station hardware.

NG-23 launch with Falcon 9 – via Jerry Pike for NSF.

Capture is planned for Dec. 1, with NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney scheduled to grapple the vehicle with Canadarm2 and berth it to the Unity module.

Jared Metter, director of flight reliability at SpaceX, noted that NG-25 will be the fifth Falcon 9 launch of a Cygnus and the third CRS cargo mission Falcon 9 has flown this year, after CRS-34 and CRS-35.

The booster for the flight is B1096 on its ninth flight, with a return to launch site landing planned at Landing Zone 40.

Northrop has not said how many more Falcon 9 flights it may ultimately need, though the sixth contracted launch suggests Antares 330 remains some way from flying Cygnus.

For now, the near-term Cygnus manifest is covered by Falcon 9, with more details on Antares 330 and NG-22 expected as Northrop works through its next vehicles.

(Lead Image: Falcon 9 with Cygnus. Credit: Sawyer Rosenstein for NSF and NASA for Cygnus)
